titre: Parkfield: The Earthquake Predicted for 1993 Arrived in 2004
accroche: In 1985, the USGS judges a magnitude 5.5 to 6 earthquake more than 90% likely before 1993. It happens on September 28, 2004.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 5, 1985, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) announces that a magnitude 5.5 to 6 earthquake is probable near Parkfield, California, with a probability of more than 90%, in the 1985-1993 window. There is nothing of divination in this announcement: it rests on a record. Earthquakes of about magnitude 6 struck Parkfield in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934, and 1966. The average interval between them is 22 years, and the seismographic recordings of the three most recent look a lot alike. Hence the hypothesis of a “characteristic” earthquake, one that would repeat almost identically.

## A Calendar, Not a Stopwatch

This prediction is the first to have been approved by the National Earthquake Prediction Evaluation Council (NEPEC) and its California counterpart. It also justifies an unprecedented setup: twenty-eight monitoring networks operate at Parkfield.

But an average hides its spread. The dates in the record give intervals of 24, 20, 21, 12, and 32 years: the shortest is almost three times shorter than the longest. Adding 22 years to 1966 gives 1988, and the 1985-1993 window surrounds that date. It is an honest bet on regularity, but a bet.

## The Window Closes

The window closes in 1993 with no earthquake of that size. Prediction attempts continue until January 2001. The earthquake comes on September 28, 2004, with a magnitude of 6.0, 38 years after the one in 1966 and eleven years after the end of the announced window. Between 1985 and 2004, no earthquake of magnitude 5.5 or greater occurred at Parkfield.

## What the Failure Left Behind

The failure of the prediction is not the failure of the experiment. The 2004 data come from geological, geodetic, seismic, magnetic, and electrical networks: it is the best-recorded earthquake to that date, and the data explain most of what happened. The authors of a special issue of the Seismological Society of America's journal nevertheless conclude that predicting the details of future earthquakes remains difficult, and that forecasting damaging shaking will probably continue to rely on probabilistic rather than deterministic methods.

The Parkfield record said the fault ruptures about every 22 years. It did not say when, to the year, and the instruments did not detect a usable precursor in 2004 either.

repere.texte: USGS prediction of April 5, 1985: a magnitude 5.5 to 6 earthquake probable at Parkfield in the 1985-1993 window, with a probability of more than 90%. Actual earthquake: September 28, 2004, magnitude 6.0.
repere.source: USGS, press release of April 5, 1985, and page “September 28, 2004, M 6.0 earthquake captured”

carte.punch: Predicted before 1993 with more than 90% probability, the Parkfield earthquake arrived in 2004.
carte.idee: Because six magnitude 6 earthquakes had struck at an average of 22 years apart (actually from 12 to 32 years), the USGS predicted in 1985 a new earthquake before 1993. It happened on September 28, 2004: an average is not a deadline.

quiz.question: Why was the Parkfield prediction for 1985-1993 a shakier bet than it looked?
choix: Because 22 years is only an average, and the actual intervals ranged from 12 to 32 years
Because the instruments of 1985 could not measure a magnitude 6 earthquake
Because the fault had never produced an earthquake of that size before 1985
Because the fault had stopped moving after the 1966 earthquake
quiz.explication: The five intervals in the record (24, 20, 21, 12, and 32 years) stray widely from their 22-year average, so an eight-year window is a bet. The record showed, on the contrary, six earthquakes of about magnitude 6 since 1857, and the fault did rupture in 2004.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis did the USGS build its 1985 prediction?
choix: A single electromagnetic signal picked up a few weeks before the 1985 announcement
A physical law giving the exact date of rupture from the length of the fault
Six similar magnitude 6 earthquakes between 1857 and 1966, spaced 22 years apart on average
A series of ten major earthquakes recorded at Parkfield between 1900 and 1980
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The record the USGS relied on is that of six similar magnitude 6 earthquakes between 1857 and 1966, with an average interval of 22 years, and not a signal, a physical law, or ten earthquakes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides being the first approved by NEPEC, what did the 1985 prediction make possible?
choix: The preventive evacuation of Parkfield's entire population
The setting up of twenty-eight monitoring networks, seismic, geodetic, and other, at Parkfield
The construction of a dam to contain possible mudflows
The installation of a single seismograph at the top of the fault
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says the 1985 prediction justified an unprecedented setup, twenty-eight monitoring networks operating at Parkfield, in addition to being the first approved by NEPEC.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the authors of the Seismological Society of America special issue conclude about the 2004 earthquake?
choix: That the 1985 deterministic prediction had in fact succeeded
That a precursor signal had indeed been detected, but too late to warn anyone
That the instruments deployed in 1985 were too few to have any chance of detecting the earthquake
That predicting the details of future earthquakes remains difficult, and that forecasting will probably continue to rely on probabilistic methods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that no usable precursor was detected in 2004, and that the authors conclude that predicting the details of earthquakes remains difficult, hence the probable reliance on probabilistic methods.
